abstract: Hyaluronan (HA) is a major component of the extracellular matrix during craniofacial development. Studies of hyaluronan synthase 2 (HAS2) have established that HA synthesis is required for normal palatal development. However, the contribution of HA degradation to this process remains poorly understood. TMEM2 is a cell-surface hyaluronidase, and previous studies have demonstrated its role in neural crest cell (NCC) migration and the survival of post-migratory NCCs. Previous Wnt1-Cre-mediated deletion of Tmem2 caused early embryonic lethality, preventing assessment of later palatal development. Here, we used Sox10-Cre to delete Tmem2 in the NCC lineage and investigate its role in palatogenesis. Conditional knockout (CKO) embryos developed complete cleft palate. Palatal shelves elevated but remained smaller than controls, with reduced proliferation and increased apoptosis. ZsGreen lineage labeling revealed reduced directional organization of NCC-derived cells, accompanied by widespread HA accumulation throughout the palatal mesenchyme. To identify molecular changes accompanying these abnormalities, we performed RNA sequencing, which revealed enrichment of hypoxia-related transcriptional programs and suppression of cell-cycle programs. Increased HIF-1? and pimonidazole labeling provided complementary evidence of tissue hypoxia. Vascular analyses revealed altered CD31-positive vessel architecture, reduced contact between NCC-derived cells and vessels, and fewer PDGFR?-positive cells. Together, these findings identify TMEM2-dependent HA remodeling as an important component of palatal development and link its disruption to altered NCC-derived mesenchymal organization, vascular and perivascular abnormalities, and tissue hypoxia.
